hook: Alex Krizhevsky was a graduate student in computer science at the University of Toronto, working under Geoffrey Hinton alongside fellow student Ilya Sutskever. In 2012 the three published ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, describing a large convolutional network, later known as AlexNet, that used GPU training and a new regularization technique to sharply cut image classification error rates. A variant of the network won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that year by a wide margin, a result widely credited with convincing the broader field that deep neural networks, trained at scale on GPUs, could outperform earlier computer vision approaches. Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton founded DNNresearch Inc. to build on the work, and in March 2013 Google acquired the company, bringing Krizhevsky and Sutskever onto Google's research staff while Hinton divided his time between Google and the university.
name: Alex Krizhevsky

reading.body:
AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet win by a wide margin convinced the broader field that GPUs could train deep neural networks to outperform earlier methods, catalyzing the modern deep learning era.

The result was not inevitable. AlexNet combined a large convolutional architecture with GPU training and a new regularization technique. The three ingredients together produced a sharp enough error reduction that the performance gap became obvious. Krizhevsky, Sutskever, and Hinton moved quickly to commercialize the insight by founding DNNresearch Inc. Google acquired the company within months in 2013, absorbing both the research and the researchers into its staff.

This sequence matters for AI infrastructure because it demonstrates how compute capability drives capability discovery. The breakthrough required not just a new algorithm but access to GPUs at the scale needed to train it. Once the field saw the results, demand for GPU compute capacity grew accordingly. The work also shows how research institutions and startups funnel talent and methods into larger technology companies, where they shape the compute and infrastructure decisions that follow.

The data does not cover how much compute AlexNet required, what its actual infrastructure footprint was, or how the acquisition changed Google's GPU procurement strategy. It establishes that the breakthrough happened, that it was GPU-dependent, and that it accelerated the field's focus on scaling neural networks. The binding constraint story runs through this data, but the data itself does not quantify the constraint.

quick_facts: Co-creator, with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, of AlexNet, described in the 2012 paper ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
A variant of AlexNet won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) in 2012 by a wide margin
Conducted the work as a graduate student in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto
Co-founded DNNresearch Inc. with Sutskever and Hinton in 2012 to commercialize the research
Joined Google's research staff after Google acquired DNNresearch Inc. in March 2013
